Our vision

AI Research is on the cusp of a new revolution.

At Perplexity Frontier Research, you can be at the forefront of driving that revolution. We believe the next big advances will come through tackling a profound open question: how do we automate scientific research?

But what defines research? Research is a cyclical process. It involves asking insightful unanswered questions, gathering what is known, noticing what isn’t, forming a hypothesis, conducting experiments, balancing uncertainty, and updating. Ultimately, research provides us with new scientifically interpretable insights. It is these insights, these theories, rather than black box predictions, which have historically been the primary quantity of interest in science. The theory of general relativity enables GPS, a powerful application, but it’s not what makes general relativity interesting: it is the understanding that space and time and gravity are all interconnected, and the whole spectrum of testable predictions that come with that understanding. While the field has advanced in making black box predictions, it has barely scratched the surface of autonomous scientific discovery.

Historically, the research loop has run inside a handful of institutions, at the speed of a few people. We think it can run inside software, for anyone.

Some agents will search wide across thousands of sources, some will go deep on one thread, others will propose experiments, others still will critique and hypothesize, all combining complementary strengths, as a whole that is far greater than the sum of its parts. This system knows what it doesn’t know, seeks out a new understanding, and remembers what it learns. In short, research is a multi-faceted effort, focused on asking the right questions and producing new scientific knowledge as an answer, with search as an integral component.

Autonomous research requires a new science of its own. Models need to generate their own training signal, keep learning after release, spend compute where information is worth the most, and coordinate across devices and datacenters as one system. This process must happen as part of a recursive self-improving loop. And these systems need fundamentally new evaluations which test for discovery, and not just recall.

We will publish papers, models, data, and benchmarks, because science compounds when it’s shared. Our research effort will also be supported by more than 10,000 GPUs. And our results end up in a product used by millions of curious people, the most challenging test of all.

The Work

Join us in reimagining the fundamental principles of intelligent systems.

Our mission to build an automated scientist involves fascinating open questions at the intersection of active learning, reasoning, synthetic data, recursive self improvement, inductive biases, and extrapolation. Within each of these efforts, we have ambitious objectives. This is an environment where you could propose the next transformer.

We will be particularly focused on pre-training, continual learning, and reinforcement learning. These are integrated efforts, unified by multi-agent orchestration. In multi-agent orchestration, our goal is to provide output that is on the Pareto frontier of quality for any cost the user wishes to spend. For example, we wish to have the best quality LLM service available at the lowest cost.

We will also be focused on designing new evaluations, quantifying what it means for a system to be good at research. Can it ask the right questions, propose experiments, autonomously improve its own abilities, to provide an interpretable scientific understanding? These evaluations will need to disambiguate reasoning versus memorization, and the quality of understanding versus mere predictive success in a task.

We aim to build a multi-agent system that takes on hard questions, does deep and wide research, gathers context about the unknown, poses questions, tests hypotheses in the real world, and keeps iterating, so that anyone can be a scientist. To get there, we particularly consider 6 areas, which each play a role in this objective:

  1. Multi-agent orchestration: asking, gathering, collaborating
  2. Pre-training: architectures that make every token count
  3. Continual learning: finding the edge of the known
  4. Reinforcement learning: hypothesize, test
  5. Systems: inference, training, environments, and security
  6. Frontier evaluations: measuring discovery

Multi-agent orchestration

  • The best quality for any cost.

Frontier models are becoming increasingly diverse. This diversity presents a distinct opportunity: by thoughtfully orchestrating multi-agent collaboration, we can create a system that is greater than the sum of its parts, and more efficient. In advisor escalation, for example, a small on-device model can ask for help from a larger model only when advantageous, providing high-quality output at a small fraction of the cost. Agentic search is another form of orchestration: a model must decide what to look for, which sources to read, and when it has enough evidence. We study how agents can make these decisions, and how retrieval models can learn to find what the agent needs next. There are many open questions at the heart of our effort: what makes a model good at orchestrating, and what belongs in the weights rather than in the harness around them? Can we develop many small specialized models that efficiently coordinate with one another? Can models communicate to one another in a more efficient language? How do we jointly train models knowing that they are being orchestrated?

Pre-training

  • Open weights
  • · New architectures
  • · Synthetic data
  • · Scaling science

We pre-train open-weight models that are efficient and specialized. Our work runs from data and mid-training curricula to new architectures, and understands how small-scale experimentation can transfer optimally to larger scales. Key questions include: can we create synthetic data that is more valuable than real data? Can we theoretically predict how small-scale experimentation will transfer to compute-optimal scaling? Can we understand what interventions will change scaling laws? Can we build small models that are state-of-the-art for specialized tasks? Can we design entirely new architectures?

Continual learning

  • Curiosity
  • · Memory
  • · Persistence
  • · Personalization

We build systems that keep learning in deployment. Curiosity is seeking out what the model does not know rather than waiting to be asked. Memory is using our experience for a head start on the next task. Persistence is staying on a job through pauses and interruptions, so progress accumulates over days instead of resetting every session. Continual learning means knowing how to continuously adapt to new environments, how to ask the right questions and seek out new information, and retaining a memory of what matters. How to ask the right questions and how to seek out new information for greater universality are particularly prescient questions at the heart of our effort.

Reinforcement learning

  • Verifiable & rubric rewards
  • · Post-training environments

Reinforcement learning at Perplexity runs against live retrieval, real products, and infrastructure that moves trillion-parameter weights from training to inference in about a second. We post-train with rewards that are verifiable where possible and rubric-graded where not, in environments synthesized from how people actually use our systems. How should a model learn when a rollout of thousands of actions returns a single sparse reward at the end? Which of those actions deserve the credit? Can synthetic environments be faithful enough that what is learned in them transfers to the live web? Can we perform pre-training interventions that make RL post-training more effective? And knowing that a reward which can be hacked eventually will be, can we design signals that survive optimization pressure?

  1. [1]JOLT: Joint On-Policy Learning and Teaching
  2. [2]Advancing Search-Augmented LMs
  3. [3]Weight Transfer in Under 2 Seconds
  4. [4]RL Training for Math Reasoning

Systems

  • Inference and training
  • · Environments and runtimes
  • · Security

The cost of training and inference depends on how models use memory and communicate between devices. Reducing the number of operations need not make a model faster if most of its time is spent moving data. We study these costs and how they should influence model design. Our work on fabric-lib provides portable communication between GPUs, while our Apple silicon engine uses kernels specialized to the model and the hardware. For agents, the system also includes the environment in which code executes. SPACE provides isolated environments that can preserve and resume an agent’s work. We study how to support long-running computation and tool use while keeping credentials and the host outside the agent’s control.

  3. [3]Making SPACE: Secure and efficient runtimes for long-running agents

Frontier evals

  • Model vs. harness
  • · Memorization vs. reasoning

There is an increasing tension between performing well on evals, and the implied general proficiency of a model. If a human wins gold on the IMO, then we expect them to be good at various other tasks where a model may profoundly fail. Part of the problem is that these evals were developed to work well as a proxy for general human ability, not for general model ability. To avoid surprising failure modes, and improve general ability, we need to quantify this gap with fundamentally new evaluations. Moreover, there is often a difference between a model’s qualitative understanding of a problem and its ability to make predictions. For example, we can train a model to predict the trajectory of a particle, but it would unlikely be able to produce equations of motions, or a theory of physics. We want to measure qualitative understanding, so that we can build systems for research that teach us something interpretable that we don’t already know. This ambition is at the core of the scientific effort. Part of evaluation also involves scientific understanding, deconstructing models, and evaluating how they generalize rather than only quantitative benchmarks. In this spirit, we are also pursuing a science of deep learning and fundamentally understanding generalization.
